pluss::timeindex::make¶

Back to TimeIndex Factory API Reference

Call Forms¶

pluss::TimeIndex pluss::timeindex::make(
    const pluss::Timeline& values,
    bool require_sorted = true)

pluss::TimeIndex pluss::timeindex::make(
    timestamp_text_input values,
    bool require_sorted = true)

pluss::TimeIndex pluss::timeindex::make(
    epoch_nanosecond_input values,
    bool require_sorted = true)

pluss::TimeIndex pluss::make_timeindex(
    const pluss::Timeline& values,
    bool require_sorted = true)

pluss::TimeIndex pluss::make_timeindex(
    timestamp_text_input values,
    bool require_sorted = true)

pluss::TimeIndex pluss::make_timeindex(
    epoch_nanosecond_input values,
    bool require_sorted = true)

timestamp_text_input includes a scalar string and a contiguous one-dimensional string range. epoch_nanosecond_input includes a scalar signed integer and a contiguous one-dimensional signed-integer range. These names describe accepted call-site concepts; no private reader type is part of the public contract.

pluss::make_timeindex(...) is the intentional root-level forwarding spelling. It has the same accepted inputs and default ordering check as pluss::timeindex::make(...); choosing it changes no storage, ownership, timezone, or validation behavior.

Promote Values Into Index Semantics¶

make() is the canonical entrance to TimeIndex. Text is parsed as timestamp instants, integers are interpreted as exact epoch nanoseconds, and an existing Timeline contributes its values and timezone. Scalar text or integer input is promoted to a one-element axis because TimeIndex is always rank one.

Construction validates the whole axis before returning it. NaT is rejected: an index position must identify an instant. An input Timeline must be rank one. With the default require_sorted=true, ticks must be non-decreasing; equal timestamps are allowed, so ordering and uniqueness remain separate contracts.

Set require_sorted=false only when unordered input must be represented long enough to call sort(), argsort(), or inspect it. Binary search, rolling, and resampling operations either require or assume increasing order and should not be applied before normalization.

Examples¶

Example 1. Scalar text becomes a one-element axis rather than a rank-zero temporal value.

auto index = pluss::timeindex::make("2025-01-01T00:00:00Z");
std::cout << pluss::timeindex::print(index) << "\n";

Output¶

TimeIndex(shape=[1], tz=UTC)
[ 2025-01-01 00:00:00 ]

Example 2. A text vector supplies the ordinary ordered-axis path.

auto index = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T01:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-01T02:00:00Z"});
std::cout << pluss::timeindex::print(index) << "\n";

Output¶

TimeIndex(shape=[3], tz=UTC)
[ 2025-01-01 00:00:00, 2025-01-01 01:00:00, 2025-01-01 02:00:00 ]

Example 3. Integer input preserves exact epoch-nanosecond identity.

auto index = pluss::timeindex::make(
    std::vector<std::int64_t>{0, 1'000'000'000LL, 2'000'000'000LL});
std::cout << pluss::timeindex::print(index) << "\n";

Output¶

TimeIndex(shape=[3], tz=UTC)
[ 1970-01-01 00:00:00, 1970-01-01 00:00:01, 1970-01-01 00:00:02 ]

Example 4. Timeline promotion preserves timezone metadata.

auto local = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2025-01-01T09:00:00", "2025-01-01T10:00:00"})
                 .tz_localize("America/Edmonton");
std::cout << pluss::timeindex::print(pluss::timeindex::make(local)) << "\n";

Output¶

TimeIndex(shape=[2], tz=America/Edmonton)
[ 2025-01-01 09:00:00, 2025-01-01 10:00:00 ]

Example 5. The root-level make_* spelling is exactly equivalent.

const auto canonical = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T01:00:00Z"});
const auto convenient = pluss::make_timeindex({
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T01:00:00Z"});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "make_timeindex_equal=" << (canonical.host() == convenient.host())
          << "\n";

Output¶

make_timeindex_equal=true

Example 6. Explicitly retain unordered input for a later ordering operation.

auto index = pluss::timeindex::make({
    "2025-01-01T02:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-01T01:00:00Z"}, false);
std::cout << pluss::timeindex::print(index) << "\n";

Output¶

TimeIndex(shape=[3], tz=UTC)
[ 2025-01-01 02:00:00, 2025-01-01 00:00:00, 2025-01-01 01:00:00 ]

Example 7. Default construction rejects that same ordering.

try {
  (void)pluss::timeindex::make({
      "2025-01-01T01:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"});
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << std::string_view(error.what()).substr(0,
      std::string_view(error.what()).find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

TimeIndex must be sorted (non-decreasing)

Example 8. A matrix Timeline cannot become a one-dimensional index.

try {
  (void)pluss::timeindex::make(pluss::timeline::make({
      {"2025-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T01:00:00Z"}}));
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << std::string_view(error.what()).substr(0,
      std::string_view(error.what()).find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

TimeIndex requires a 1D Timeline

Ownership And Cost¶

Text and integer call forms allocate TimeIndex storage. Timeline promotion shares already packed tick storage through the underlying reference-counted Series; a strided Timeline is materialized once so subsequent ordered kernels can scan packed memory safely. Validation is O(n) and does not reorder input.
